project.name: treetracker-web-map-client
project.description: Displays location and details of all trees tracked in the Greenstand reforestation network, powering the public web map at treetracker.org. It is a Next.js and React single-page application that renders tree, planter, organization, and wallet data on an interactive Leaflet map.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: The README explains what this project does: it renders every tree tracked by the Greenstand reforestation network on an interactive map at treetracker.org. It documents the local dev setup (Node 16, npm run dev), the TDD workflow with Cypress, and conventions for building components and pages. Use it as the map for the rest of this tour: it names most of the concepts you are about to see in code.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: _app.js is the Next.js custom App component that every page in this project passes through. It wraps each page with the authentication, theme, drawer, and map providers, sets up an Emotion cache for Material UI's server-side styles, wires Google Analytics and web-vitals reporting, and can optionally boot an MSW mock server for local development. Reading this file first tells you exactly which subsystems exist before you see any of them individually.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js custom App components (_app.js) are the single place to inject providers that must wrap every page; anything not composed here has to be re-added page by page.

tour.title: Tech Stack & Dependencies
tour.description: package.json reveals the technology choices behind the providers you just saw in _app.js: Leaflet-based mapping comes through the shared treetracker-web-map-core package, Material UI supplies the design system, Keycloak handles authentication, and Mock Service Worker (MSW) fakes the backend during development and tests. The Node 16 engine pin and browserslist targets explain some of the project's build constraints mentioned in the README.

tour.title: The Map Domain Model
tour.description: mapContext.js exposes the shared Leaflet map instance to the whole component tree through a React context, while MapModel.js is the core domain model wrapping that map instance: it tracks markers and viewport, and implements the directional-arrow algorithm that points users toward the nearest tree outside the visible bounds. Together these two files are the foundation every map-aware component in the app builds on.

tour.title: Fetching Domain Data
tour.description: api.js centralizes every axios-based HTTP call to the treetracker backend, fetching trees, organizations, planters, growers, wallets, and tokens. entity.js layers a smaller, focused API client on top for fetching a single map entity by id, wallet name, or map name. These two files are how the app turns raw backend data into the objects the map and detail pages render.
tour.languageLesson: Centralizing HTTP calls in one module (rather than scattering fetch calls across components) keeps the API contract in one place and makes it easy to swap in the MSW mocks you saw referenced in _app.js.

tour.title: URL as Application State
tour.description: pathResolver.js resolves and updates the browser URL as users interact with the map: clicking a tree, panning, or zooming all rewrite the path and query string so the current view is shareable and restorable from a link alone. With the highest fan-out among application code files, it is the glue between the map's live interaction state (Step 4) and Next.js routing.

tour.title: Responsive Layouts
tour.description: The app renders three different layout shells depending on context. Layout.js is the desktop split-pane view with a Navbar, scrollable content panel, and the map. LayoutMobile.js stacks a dynamically-loaded Navbar and Drawer over a full-screen map for small viewports. LayoutEmbed.js is used when the map is embedded in a third party page, combining a collapsible drawer with search and timeline controls. All three compose around the same map instance from Step 4.

tour.title: Navigation & the Details Drawer
tour.description: Navbar.js renders the top navigation bar with the Treetracker logo, configurable nav links, and a theme toggle, hiding itself automatically in embed mode. Drawer.js is the swipeable bottom-sheet used on mobile to show tree, planter, or organization details, implemented with custom touch-drag handling for open and close gestures. Both are composed into the layouts from Step 7.

tour.title: Entity Detail Pages
tour.description: These four Next.js dynamic routes are where a map marker becomes a full detail view: a tree's photo, species, and capture location; a planter's profile; an organization's page; and a wallet's holdings. Each uses getStaticProps/getStaticPaths for build-time data fetching through the api.js client from Step 5, and each is exercised by its own Cypress integration test you would find under cypress/tests/integration.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js bracket syntax in a filename, like [treeid].js, declares a dynamic route segment; the value is available to the page via useRouter or getStaticPaths params.

tour.title: The Search Feature
tour.description: Search.js is the container component that manages search keyword, results, and focus state, switching between live results and recent search history stored in localStorage. SearchInput.js is the debounced text field driving it. mockApi.js stands in for a real search backend today, providing a static in-memory dataset filtered by keyword, showing how UI features can be built and tested ahead of a real API being ready.

tour.title: Admin Dashboard Configuration
tour.description: dashboardContext.js holds the admin dashboard's editable configuration state (navbar branding, initial map view), backed by a reducer and persisted to local storage. config.reducer.js implements that reducer's actions: logo URL changes, navbar item CRUD and reordering, and map location updates. global.js is the admin page that ties them together, fetching an organization's settings server-side and syncing them into this shared state.

tour.title: Theming System
tour.description: themeContext.js builds the Material UI theme object for light and dark mode and provides a CustomThemeProvider that loads persisted or server-supplied theme overrides. admin/theme.js is the live playground built on top of it: an iframe preview alongside palette, typography, and font controls, gated behind a Keycloak entitlement check, that lets an organization customize and save its own branding.

tour.title: The API Contract
tour.description: This OpenAPI specification documents the Greenstand web-map information API that api.js (Step 5) and entity.js consume: endpoints for trees, planters, species, organizations, and wallets, shared by this client, the wallet app, and other consumers. It is the authoritative contract behind every fetch call you traced through the data layer.
tour.languageLesson: OpenAPI specs enforce the shape of requests and responses at the schema level, letting frontend and backend teams work against a shared contract instead of tribal knowledge.

tour.title: Containerization, Deployment & CI
tour.description: The Dockerfile packages the Next.js production build into a node:16-alpine image, installing dependencies and running npm run start. The Kubernetes Deployment manifest describes how that image runs in the cluster, including environment variables pointing at the right API and tile server for each environment. The pull-request-ci.yml workflow is the quality gate that runs before any of this ships: Cypress integration and component tests, Jest unit tests, and ESLint, all in parallel jobs.
tour.languageLesson: Kustomize overlays layer environment-specific patches (dev, test, prod) on top of a shared base manifest, avoiding duplicated YAML across environments.
